chunks.content: 1 Introduction Prostate cancer (PCa) is the most common non-skin cancer and the leading cause of cancer deaths in 48 countries, and it has been identified as the fifth leading cause of death worldwide [ ]. Age, African-American race, family history, and germline mutations are well-established nonmodifiable risk factors for PCa, and metabolic syndrome, excessive body weight, and smoking have been identified as potential modifiable risk factors [ , ]. The incidence and mortality among black men compared to white men are 1.7 and 2.1 times as high as those among white men, respectively [ ]. The majority of new cases are diagnosed in 65–74 year-old men, and it is a very uncommon cancer in men younger than 45 years old. Autopsy studies show that up to 80% of men will harbor PCa by the age of 80 years old; however, most such cancers are slow-growing, low-grade, relatively harmless, and have little impact on survival in this age group [ ]. The aggressiveness of PCa is highly variable and largely depends on the initial grade at diagnosis. Patients with a Gleason score of 8–10 (Grade Groups 3–5) can progress from localized disease to metastasis and death within a relatively short time period, whereas patients with a Gleason score of 6 (Grade Group 1) may never experience symptoms or disease progression [ ]. PCa can be detected at an early, asymptomatic stage, while it is still curable. This is called screening. Screening for PCa has been primarily based on prostate-specific antigen (PSA), with the objective of detecting PCa in its early stages, thereby reducing PCa-specific mortality [ ]. A recent systematic review showed that the digital rectal examination has a notably low diagnostic value as an independent screening test or supplement to PSA (positive predictive value 21%); however, it is an essential part of clinical work-up of elevated PSA [ ]. Therefore, PSA is the primary screening test for PCa. However, PCa screening remains controversial, with varying recommendations among medical societies and governments [ ]. This controversy arises from concerns about potential overdiagnosis and overtreatment of low-risk PCa, complications from unnecessary biopsies, and the magnitude of benefits derived from early diagnosis and treatment in relation to the potential harm. Surgery and radiation therapy are the main treatment modalities for localized PCa, generally resulting in successful outcomes but carrying the risk of harms, such as erectile dysfunction or urinary incontinence [ , ]. Over the past few years, active surveillance has emerged as an alternative initial management strategy for individuals with PCa of low or low-intermediate risk [ ]. Additionally, several new diagnostic modalities, such as MRI and MRI-targeted biopsy, biomarkers in blood and urine, and tools for individual risk stratification, have entered the clinical landscape of screening and early detection of PCa. This comprehensive review aims to provide the current evidence of PCa screening. The purpose of this review article is to summarize the Level I evidence from randomized controlled trials of PSA screening and treatment for PCa [ ]. 2 Methods A narrative review of randomized controlled trials of PCa screening and treatment was performed. We restricted this review to population-based trials enrolling men at average risk of PCa, i.e. , trials conducted in the general population and not specifically targeting men with specific factors that increase their likelihood of developing PCa compared to the general male population. We retrieved full-text articles of the most recent follow-up publications from the trials based on our extensive expert knowledge of the literature. We did not conduct a formal database search with specific keywords because our familiarity with the key papers in this field allowed us to directly identify the relevant and most up-to-date publications. After data collection, an expert informationist was consulted to conduct a literature search to identify any missed relevant and recent studies, by searching for trials started between 2014 and 2023 using ClinicalTrials.gov, International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), and International Standard Randomised Controlled Trial Number (ISRCTN). The search confirmed that no recent trials or later publications had been missed. 3 PSA as a screening tool PSA, discovered in 1979 and first used clinically in the late 1980s, has become the primary tool for detecting, staging, and monitoring PCa [ ]. Once inside, it undergoes a conversion into active PSA, ultimately breaching the capillary membranes to access the systemic circulation. Following its generation within cells, pro-PSA traverses the basal and endothelial cell layers before entering the ducts of the prostate. Once inside, it undergoes a conversion into active PSA, ultimately breaching the capillary membranes to access the systemic circulation. A fraction of this active PSA then experiences proteolysis, transforming into an inactive or “free” PSA upon entry into the bloodstream, where it remains unbound. Active PSA that reaches the bloodstream quickly binds to circulating protease inhibitors. The age-adjusted percentage ratio of free to protein-bound PSA serves as a valuable indicator of PCa, given that the ratio of free PSA to total PSA tends to decrease in cases of malignancy [ ]. Using measurements of concentrations of PSA as a PCa screening tool remains a topic of debate when considering healthy, asymptomatic males. This is due to the fact that elevated serum PSA levels are detected in numerous benign prostatic conditions. Conditions such as benign prostatic hyperplasia, infection, inflammation, or trauma can cause an increase in serum PSA levels, thereby diminishing the specificity of this biomarker as a test to detect PCa [ ]. However, the baseline PSA concentration in midlife has been demonstrated to be a strong prognostic marker of future risk of lethal PCa and can also be used to exclude men at increased risk. For example, men with a PSA level below 1 ng/mL have a very low 25-year risk of developing metastatic PCa or dying from the disease [ ]. Although there is no specific PSA level below which PCa can be ruled out, a PSA level above 3 ng/mL is commonly used to recommend further evaluation ( e.g. , repeating the PSA, performing a digital rectal examination, and considering risk calculators, reflex biomarkers, and/or MRI) before deciding to proceed to a prostate biopsy. 4 Randomized controlled PSA screening trials A summary of the randomized controlled trials of screening and treatment for PCa has been published previously [ ]. In essence, the collective evidence from the screening trials demonstrates that regular PSA screening leads to a reduction in PCa mortality, though the benefits must be weighed against the risks of overdiagnosis and overtreatment. Treatment trials indicate that while prostatectomy and radiation therapy provide excellent outcomes, they are associated with significant risks such as urinary incontinence, erectile dysfunction, and bowel dysfunction [ ]. In detail, four contemporary, high-quality, randomized controlled trials have assessed the effectiveness of a PSA-based screening program on PCa-mortality, representing the available evidence with the most recent follow-up ( ). The multicenter European Randomized Study of Screening for Prostate Cancer (ERSPC) began in the early 90s and enrolled men in nine European countries. The study involved 162 389 men aged 55–69 years old (core age group), and results after a follow-up period of 16 years are currently available [ , ]. The screening group was invited to a blood sample screening protocol every 2–4 years, with a PSA cutoff of 3 ng/mL in most centers to recommend a systematic biopsy, while the control group was not invited to screening (but had some exposure to opportunistic PSA testing in later years of the trial). PCa-specific mortality, the primary outcome, was significantly lower in men who underwent screening compared to the control group: risk ratio (RR) 0.80 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.72–0.89, p <0.001) at 16 years of follow-up. As the absolute benefit and follow-up time increase, the number needed to invite (NNI) and the number needed to diagnose (NND) to prevent one PCa death have been decreasing over time. In the last update at 16 years, the reported values were 570 and 18, respectively [ ], as opposed to the initial follow-up (9 years) values of 1410 and 48, respectively [ ]. Similarly, when the follow-up is extended to 25 years in modeling studies, the NNI and NND decrease to 385 and 11, respectively [ ]. The ERSPC also demonstrates the importance of dynamic, repeated screening. There was a 25% reduction in PCa mortality for those who attended only one screening round, as opposed to a 48% reduction for those who attended at least twice. This difference is explained by the fact that men diagnosed in the first round tended to have incurable disease (prevalence screening), which was much less common in subsequent screening rounds. The 20% reduction in PCa-specific mortality is further substantiated by the Göteborg-1 trial, with an independent study protocol, part of which was included in the ERSPC (the core age group), presenting the longest available follow-up results to date (22 years), and reporting a 77% attendance rate in the screening group (having a PSA-test at least once) [ ]. An observed benefit in PCa mortality for the screening group amounted to an approximate 30% reduction (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.55–0.91, p =0.005), with an NNI of 217 and NND of nine. This also represents a decrease from earlier follow-up data (previously 293 and 12, respectively, at 14 years of follow-up) and a larger absolute risk reduction. While a decreasing relative mortality risk reduction was reported over longer follow-up periods (RR 0.71 at 22 years; 0.55 at 14 years), the investigators explained this finding by noting that men in the screening program, on average, stopped screening at 69 years, later constituting a significant portion of PCa deaths in the study group, and there was also increased exposure to opportunistic screening in the control arm. An increased risk of PCa death was reported in men with more than 10 years of follow-up after screening termination, those entering the program after age 60 years, and those who did not undergo testing [ ]. In contrast to these results, the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian (PLCO) trial, conducted in the United States, initiated in 1993 with the participation of 76 683 men aged 55–74 years, did not show a statistically significant reduction in PCa mortality following a screening protocol compared to usual care. The screening group underwent annual PSA testing and digital rectal examination for 6 years and 4 years, respectively, while the control group received standard practice, which also included PSA testing. The PSA cutoff for recommending a biopsy was set at 4 ng/mL, and follow-up was at the discretion of the men's primary care physicians, with PCa mortality as the primary outcome. The RR for PCa mortality was 0.93 (95% CI 0.81–1.08, p =0.38) at 17 years [ , ]. The main reason that the trial did not detect a difference in PCa mortality between trial arms was the high extent of contamination, i.e. , PSA-testing in the control group, which reduced the statistical power [ ], with 86% of control men undergoing any PSA testing during the trial and nearly half (46%) receiving annual PSA testing (in contrast to approximately 20% contamination in the ERSPC trial). Moreover, the rates of biopsy compliance in men with abnormal PSA levels were 64% in the PLCO experimental group compared to 86% in the ERSPC study. When accounting for contamination in both the ERSPC and PLCO, modeling studies have demonstrated that regular PSA screening in these trials reduced PCa mortality by 30% at 11 years of follow-up [ ]. The impact of a low-intensity PSA screening was assessed in the UK Cluster Randomized Trial of PSA Testing for Prostate Cancer (CAP). A total of 419 582 men were randomized to either a one-time PSA screening test or no screening. A prostate biopsy recommendation was made if PSA levels were ≥3.0 ng/mL. Following a median follow-up of 10 years, no significant difference in PCa mortality was found (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.85–1.08, p =0.50) [ ]. Additionally, a higher number of low-risk PCa cases were identified in the intervention group. However, at 15 years of follow-up, there was a statistically significant reduction in PCa mortality in the intervention group compared to the control group (RR 0.92 [95% CI 0.85–0.99], p =0.03), albeit smaller than other screening trials [ ]. The CAP study has been criticized for using a one-time screening PSA, low adherence to biopsy recommendations, with only 40% of patients in the intervention group complying. Moreover, the use of a single screening round, as established in other studies such as the first round of the Göteborg-1 trial, has been noted to detect more advanced and incurable cancers compared to dynamic screening at regular screening intervals. In addition to these conflicting trial results, PCa screening is associated with potential physical and psychological harms. The transrectal and transperineal biopsy techniques carry a risk of hematuria, hematospermia, dysuria, pain, and infection (5%–7%), which poses a major risk and is the primary cause of hospitalization (1%–5%) [ ]. Nevertheless, once diagnosed with PCa, a man faces the risk of overtreatment of the indolent disease, which can vary between series [ ]. In the USA, the rate of active surveillance for low-risk PCa varies between 4% and 78% depending on many factors including the year of diagnosis (more surveillance in recent years) [ ]. 5 Implementing risk-stratification, biomarkers, and MRI in screening pathways Recent advancements in PCa screening emphasize a risk-adapted strategy using PSA testing alongside factors like age, family history, and PSA density to better stratify risk. Multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) is now recommended before a biopsy to target specific areas and reduce unnecessary procedures. New biomarkers and risk calculators can improve accuracy and minimize false positives. Reflex testing after an initial PSA helps avoid overdiagnosis. Artificial intelligence is being integrated to enhance detection and interpretation. Despite challenges in implementation, these approaches aim for personalized and effective early detection while reducing harms associated with overdiagnosis and overtreatment. The PRAISE-U initiative is a project funded by the European Union to promote a risk-adapted approach to PCa screening across Europe. PRAISE-U aims to implement a more personalized and stratified screening strategy, utilizing tools such as PSA density, risk calculators, and mpMRI, to improve the effectiveness of PCa detection while minimizing unnecessary procedures and overdiagnosis. The initiative also focuses on ensuring appropriate infrastructure, training, and quality assurance to support the integration of these new screening methods into healthcare systems [ ]. MRI has emerged in the past years as an important tool in the diagnostic pathway of PCa and could impact the future screening recommendations. MRI with targeted biopsies to suspicious lesions on MRI has shown potential in the PCa screening and diagnosis pathway. In a recent Cochrane meta-analysis and database review comparing MRI to template biopsies, MRI demonstrated a pooled sensitivity of 0.91 and a pooled specificity of 0.37 for the International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP) Grade Group ≥2, as well as a pooled sensitivity of 0.95 and a pooled specificity of 0.35 for ISUP grade ≥3. MRI performs best when the PCa diameter is larger than 10 mm [ ]. Additionally, pivotal studies like the PRECISION trial have shown that MRI-targeted biopsies reduce the detection of ISUP Grade Group 1 PCa compared to systematic biopsies (9% vs. 22%, p >0.001) [ ]. These results support the idea of avoiding overdiagnosis and, consequently, overtreating patients by refraining from diagnosing low-risk PCa. Randomized trials have evaluated the implementation of MRI in screening programs ( ). The Stockholm-3 trial was a population-based non-inferiority trial that invited men aged 50–74 years. Those with PSA levels ≥3 ng/mL or a Stockholm-3 test ≥11% (a multiplex test including PSA and other isoforms, clinical and genetic information) were randomly assigned to undergo either a standard biopsy (10–12 cores) or an MRI, along with standard and targeted biopsies in the presence of suspicious lesions. However, only patients with PSA ≥3 ng/mL were included in the final analysis. Within the MRI group, individuals with negative results for clinically significant lesions did not undergo biopsies, except for those with a Stockholm-3 score ≥25%, for whom a standard biopsy was performed. The primary outcome measured was the proportion of clinically significant cancer detected. The results indicated that MRI with targeted and standard biopsies was non-inferior to standard biopsies in detecting clinically significant PCa. In the intention-to-treat analysis, clinically significant cancer was diagnosed in 21% of men in the experimental group and 18% in the control group. Additionally, the percentage of clinically insignificant PCa was lower in the experimental biopsy group compared to the standard biopsy group (4% vs. 12%). The authors reported a 48% lower incidence of patients undergoing biopsies, 73% fewer biopsies with benign findings and 62% fewer clinically significant cancers detected when using an MRI-pathway when normalized to a population of 10 000 men (50–74 years) [ ]. Similarly, the ProScreen randomized trial, conducted in Finland with 61 193 men aged 50–63 years, evaluated the efficacy of a PCa screening protocol involving PSA testing, the 4-kallikrein panel, and MRI. Among those invited for screening, there was a higher detection of high-grade PCa (1.13%) compared to the control group (0.62%), with an additional one case of high-grade cancer detected per 196 men screened. Low-grade PCa detection was also higher in the invited group (0.26%) compared to the control group (0.14%), with an additional one case of low-grade cancer detected per 909 men screened. These findings are preliminary, and the report of primary PCa mortality outcome of the trial is pending [ ]. The prostate MRI versus PSA screening for PCa detection (the MVP Study), on the other hand, was the first randomized trial to compare PSA testing and prostate MRI for PCa screening. In this study, 525 patients were randomized between MRI and PSA testing. A cut-off of 2.6 ng/mL in the control group and a Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PIRADS) 4–5 MRI in the experimental group were established as biopsy recommendations. The MRI protocol resulted in fewer biopsy recommendations (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.33–0.82, p =0.005), although the total PCa detection, and clinically significant PCa detected, did not reach statistical significance (RR of clinically significant PCa 2.77, 95% CI 0.89–8.59, p =0.07). The study was prematurely terminated due to recruitment challenges during the COVID-19 pandemic, resulting in the study being underpowered [ ]. Moving forward in the effort to reduce the overdiagnosis of low-risk cancer, the Göteborg-2 study investigated whether omitting systematic biopsies for men with an elevated PSA level (≥3 ng/mL) and conducting targeted biopsies of MRI-positive lesions could decrease the risk of detecting clinically insignificant PCa while maintaining the detection of clinically significant PCa. The study took place in a single academic center with double reading of MRI. Men aged 50–70 years were invited to participate in the screening program, with 17 980 individuals taking part in the trial. The experimental group showed a significant reduction in the detection rate of non-significant PCa (ISUP 1), cut by half (RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.33–0.64, p <0.001). The detection rate of ISUP ≥2 cancers was similar between trial arms (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.60–1.10) [ ]. A recent UK cohort study, ReIMAGINE, invited men aged 50–74 years to undergo MRI screening and PSA testing. Those with a positive MRI or elevated PSA density were recommended for the National Health Service PCa assessment. Among the 303 patients who completed the screening, 16% showed positive MRI findings. After the National Health Service referral, 9.6% of patients were diagnosed with clinically significant PCa compared to a 1% diagnosis of clinically insignificant PCa. Over half of the men with significant PCa on biopsies had a PSA level of 3 ng/mL (60%). This study could leverage targeted histological data from MRI-era cohorts to enhance current risk models, which are primarily based on transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy data [ ]. While the recent significant results are standardizing the use of pre-biopsy MRI in PCa early detection pathways, the utilization of population-based PCa screening solely relying on MRI is not well-developed and, as a result, remains unestablished. Several factors such as the restricted accessibility, radiologists’ expertise dependence, elevated cost of multiparametric MRI, and the time-consuming nature of MRI limit its application. 6 PCa treatment trials When it comes to the treatment of patients diagnosed with PCa, a fundamental question arises: what is the evidence that radical treatment improves survival? Three pivotal trials have been undertaken to help inform our practice in this regard: the Scandinavian Prostate Cancer Group 4 (SPCG-4) [ , ], the Prostate Cancer Intervention versus Observation Trial (PIVOT) [ , ], and the Prostate Testing for Cancer and Treatment (ProtecT) trial [ , ] ( ). Among these trials, the SPCG-4 study stands out as the sole unequivocally positive trial, characterized by pre-dating the PSA screening era and predominantly enrolling patients with palpable disease during digital rectal exams. It should also be considered that mean PSA levels were elevated in these two trials (13 ng/mL in the SPCG-4 and 10 ng/mL in the PIVOT), potentially resulting in understaging compared to current protocols; consequently, the outcomes might be even better nowadays. On the flip side, contemporary treatments for advanced PCa provide enhanced survival, prompting the debate about whether the benefits seen in these trials would remain in the presence of superior therapeutic options after disease progression (docetaxel, cabazitaxel, new hormonal agents, etc. ). The PIVOT was similar to the SPCG-4, methodologically, and recruited a comparable population (45% low risk, 35% intermediate risk, and 20% high risk), yet 50% were diagnosed after PSA screening (compared to 12% in the SPCG-4), and radical prostatectomy did not significantly reduce PCa mortality or all-cause mortality compared with conservative management after 18.6 years of follow-up [ ]. This means that men with low-risk and low-PSA disease are good candidates for active surveillance, as is now the preferred care option for these men in urology guidelines [ ]. The ProtecT trial, the most contemporaneous trial, included a lower-risk cohort, with 75% diagnosed through PSA screening. Notably, patients were 77% low risk, 20% intermediate risk, 3% high risk, with a lower mean PSA value (5.8 ng/mL), and generally younger and healthier compared to the SPCG-4 and PIVOT cohorts [ , ]. In summary, these trials reveal a statistically significant advantage of radical prostatectomy over observation for the treatment of intermediate-risk PCa but without reaching clinical significance in the PIVOT and ProtecT trials. While the benefit for low-risk and high-risk patients remains more debatable concerning PCa mortality, the potential delay in metastasis development emerges as a clinically relevant outcome to include in shared decision-making with our patients. Future trials incorporating current management paradigms (multiparametric MRI, fusion biopsy, prostate-specific membrane antigen positron emission tomography, new antiandrogen therapies, etc. ) are needed to determine if active treatment truly prolongs survival in PCa patients diagnosed through PSA screening in the modern era. 7 PCa screening and society guidelines' position A summary of the main urological guidelines' recommendations is included in [ , , , , ]. A general consensus emphasizes the importance of not initiating PSA screening without prior discussion of its potential harms and benefits with men. The screening interval is established by considering PSA baseline levels and risk calculators, and is extended until a life expectancy of 10–15 years is reached. Early and more frequent PSA testing is recommended in cases with a high risk of PCa. Accepted high-risk factors include a family history of PCa, African descent, and BRCA2 mutations or other germline mutations. 8 The future: a risk-adapted strategy of combined factors Currently, there are multiple diagnostic tools available to assess the necessity of a biopsy, incorporating clinical data with PSA levels. They encompass demographic factors, race, family history, imaging (ultrasound and MRI), PSA, percent free PSA, prostate volume, PSA density, and the history of prior biopsies, among other considerations, including risk calculators and blood or urine biomarkers. While their use has been expanding in medical practice, it is important to note that risk calculators require calibration and consideration for differences in geographical populations [ ]. Early detection is recommended to lead to a significant reduction in mortality in screening programs. However, the NNI and NND, along with concerns about overdiagnosis and associated harms, highlight the need for improved accuracy in screening approaches before implementing them in the general population. Various strategies have been proposed in this regard. Retrospective observations on participants in, for example, the Malmo Preventive Project, a Swedish cardiovascular study conducted from 1974 to 1986, indicated that PSA levels at early ages (44–50 years) were a robust predictor of PCa up to 20 years later. Specifically, 81% of the PCa diagnosed at an advanced stage were found in men with early-baseline PSA levels above the age-specific median (>0.63 ng/mL) [ ]. These findings suggest the possibility of implementing a risk-adapted screening strategy, adjusting the frequency based on the early baseline PSA level. Furthermore, in this context, the recent Prostate Cancer Early Detection Study Based on a Baseline PSA Value in Young Men (PROBASE trial), a prospective randomized trial, compared immediate early PSA assessment at age 45 years versus deferred PSA evaluation at age 50 years in 46 642 participants. Other potential approaches for new screening methods include the utilization of multi-kallikrein panels or RNA-urine tests. The ProScreen study, a screening trial employing PSA followed by a 4-kallikrein panel and MRI, has recently conducted a feasibility evaluation in a sample of 400 men demonstrating proof-of-principle of a risk-stratified screening pathway and fewer men referred to a prostate biopsy using three screening tests (results pending from the ongoing large-scale trial) [ ]. In contrast, the ongoing BARCODE-1 trial, which has also recently published its feasibility evaluation, aims to assess a PCa screening program by selecting men based on their genetic risk of PCa using DNA extraction from saliva samples [ ]. In addition, population-based organized testing programs are currently being evaluated across 12 countries in the European Union within the PRAISE-U Consortium, to determine the implementation and cost-effectiveness of risk-stratified screening strategies [ ]. 9 Conclusion PCa screening has demonstrated a benefit in terms of reducing PCa mortality after 10 years of follow-up. Nevertheless, its application is not without risks, so a shared decision-making process must be ensured between the patient and the clinician before ordering the PSA test. Emerging tools such as MRI, genetic panels, and new biomarkers show promising opportunities to reduce these harms and the overdiagnosis of low-risk cancers. 1 Introduction Radical nephrectomy and inferior vena cava (IVC) thrombectomy provide reasonable long-term survival rates for patients with renal cancer and IVC thrombus [ , , ]. Surgical strategies included cavotomy, cavectomy, and partial IVC wall resection, according to the characteristics of the IVC thrombus [ , , , ]. Our team has reported a preoperative decision-making scheme for surgical strategies for cavectomy or thrombectomy based on factors such as the affected kidney side, establishment of collaterals, and IVC wall invasion [ ]. Among those factors, invasion of the IVC wall is the most important factor affecting surgical techniques for resection and cancer-specific survival [ , , ]. The involved IVC wall should be resected using cavectomy or partial IVC wall resection, depending on the extent of the lesion [ , , ]. However, techniques that can accurately predict preoperative IVC wall invasion are not well developed. In this study, a virtual vascular endoscopy was used to identify IVC wall invasion preoperatively. The accuracy of the technique and surgical and survival outcomes were also analysed. 2 Patients and methods 2.1 Patients A total of 36 patients with renal tumors and IVC thrombi who underwent CT and subsequent robot-assisted IVC thrombectomy (RA-IVCT) between June 2016 and March 2022 at the Chinese PLA General Hospital, Beijing, China were included. Virtual vascular endoscopy was performed to identify IVC invasion based on preoperative CT. All patients underwent multiparameter MRI within 1 week before surgery. If the IVC thrombus breaches the vessel wall and imaging reveals a loss of vessel wall delineation or heterogeneous enhancement of the wall, IVC wall invasion is presumed to be present [ , ]. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Chinese PLA General Hospital (internal registration No. S2018-219-01). Written informed consent was obtained from all the patients. 2.2 Deep learning of virtual vascular endoscopy 2.2.1 Data requirements Virtual images were reconstructed using preoperative CT, and the parameters are shown in . 2.2.2 Main technology of virtual vascular endoscopy The core algorithm for virtual vascular endoscopy is illustrated in . During the reconstruction process, the Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine datasets were streamed into the deep learning models. The models then learn the import features for each organ based on previous datasets and evolve to achieve higher image accuracy. The middle datasets were subsequently used to produce a realistic image reconstruction, which can be viewed through digital virtual reality. The system architecture is described in the patent reference (Patent No.: US10713856B2). The renal tumor, thrombus, and IVC wall features were learned concentratedly. 2.2.3 Models for predicting IVC wall invasion Two major models are used for predicting IVC wall invasion. The first model focuses on image segmentation. This deep learning model learns the features of the kidney, renal tumor, IVC thrombus, and IVC wall by accurately labelling every pixel of the whole-body CT dataset for reconstruction. Invaded IVC wall has very similar imaging features to non-invaded IVC wall. Because there is a relatively small number of invaded pixels, higher accuracy is needed. The second classification model supplements the first and classifies each pixel individually, providing a positive or negative assessment. 1 Introduction Bladder cancer (BC) is the 7th most commonly diagnosed cancer in males, whilst it drops to the 10th position when both genders are considered [ ]. In non-metastatic BC, approximately 75% of patients present with disease confined to the mucosa (pTa, carcinoma in situ [CIS]) or submucosa (pT1), but most of the cancer-specific mortality is associated with pT2–T4 tumors [ ]. The current treatment of clinically non-metastatic muscle-invasive BC (MIBC) is associated with significant morbidity and mortality [ , ]. Since it generally affects elderly people with more comorbidities, postoperative complications are more likely to occur [ ]. MIBC only reaches a 50% 5-year survival rate [ , ], despite aggressive treatment with radical cystectomy (RC) and pelvic lymph node dissection, currently being the gold-standard approach [ , , , , , , ]. RC is related to infectious, genitourinary, gastrointestinal, and wound-related complications, occurring in up to 58% and perisurgical mortality up to 4.7% (at 90 days) of patients with MIBC [ ]. Additionally, sexual function and social and/or economic aspects have a significant impact on quality of life (QoL) [ , ]. All of these complications reflect the need for bladder-sparing options for non-metastatic MIBC [ ]. Several bladder-sparing therapies have been described, including chemotherapy (CMT), radiotherapy (RT), and trimodality therapy (TMT) [ ]. RT alone has been shown to have worse outcomes when compared to chemoradiotherapy and TMT [ , ]. On the other hand, CMT has shown a limited role as a single or dual therapy compared to TMT [ ]. While all monotherapies are less effective than RC and are not recommended as curative therapy [ , , ], TMT has shown favorable results. In fact, TMT, which consists of maximal transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) followed by RT with concurrent radiosensitizing CMT, is currently the most common bladder preservation strategy [ ]. Immunotherapy (IMT) agents such as immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have provided new perspectives in the treatment of MIBC during the last years [ ]. Among them, inhibitors of programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1), programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1), and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated antigen 4 (CTLA-4) are currently available therapies with different results and indications [ ]. Among the limitations of bladder-sparing strategies, the evidence is still limited and heterogeneous in the population and inclusion criteria. Additionally, cohorts are small and do not have long-term follow-up, and there are no prospective randomized studies comparing outcomes between RC and TMT. Reviews and meta-analyses published to date provide discordant results that preclude drawing concrete conclusions about therapies [ , , ]. In addition, IMT is a developing alternative for which few published results exist and have not yet been included in reviews as a therapy alone [ ]. The aim of this study was to systematically analyze the most recent scientific literature regarding organ preservation strategies in the treatment of non-metastatic MIBC, comparing oncologic and functional outcomes, and QoL between RC and TMT, in addition to results of novel IMT agents for BC. Additionally, a meta-analysis was performed to compare the 5-year overall survival (OS) outcomes between both treatments across multiple studies, enhancing the quality of the conclusions. 2 Acquisition of evidence and analyses The literature search was conducted using PubMed (access date: August 27, 2023), Google Scholar (access date: September 3, 2023), EMBASE (access date: September 11, 2023), Wiley Library (access date: September 11, 2023), and ClinicalTrials.gov (access date: October 19, 2023). Introduction Glucose-regulated protein 78 (GRP78) is a member of the HSP70 (heat shock protein 70) super family, which is found in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) lumen. The main functions of GRP78 are protein assembly, folding, and transfer to its functional site in the ER membrane. Other tasks of GRP78 include targeting incorrectly folded proteins for proteasomal degradation and regulating calcium homeostasis in normal cells. , Multiple studies have reported surface overexpression of GRP78 in many cancer types. Studies show GRP78 expression is highly increased in proliferating cancer cells and tumor-related endothelium. This is in response to stress caused by severe lactic acidosis, hypoxia, and glucose starvation (tumor microenvironment characteristics). In cancer cells, ER membrane-spanning GRP78 is transported to the cell surface. This phenomenon is unique to cancer and rarely observed in normal cells. The level of expression and surface translocation is often correlated with the rate of proliferation, malignancy, anti-apoptotic activity, drug resistance, and metastasis. - Many cancer types, such as breast cancer, hepatoma, melanoma, pancreatic cancer, and osteosarcoma, have elevated GRP78 surface expression. These findings indicate cell surface GRP78 is a promising cancer cell-specific biomarker and a beneficial target for cancer treatment. , Metastatic cancer cells express high levels of GRP78 on the cell surface, and this high expression is associated with lymph node metastasis. Specifically, in breast cancer (BC), it was found that high levels of cell surface GRP78 promote high phosphorylation rates of STAT3 and boost cancer cell growth and migration. Cell surface GRP78 can function either to activate apoptotic or anti-apoptotic signaling pathways in cancer cells. GRP78 autoantibodies such as C38 that target the C-terminus domain of the protein can activate the P53 apoptotic signaling pathway and start apoptosis, resulting in tumor growth inhibition. This further highlights the importance of targeting GRP78 to inhibit the growth and metastasis of cancer cells. The C-terminal of GRP78 is a convenient target for developing inhibitory antibodies or vaccines in cancer patients. BC is the most common malignancy in women and the second leading cause of cancer death worldwide. One in nine women will develop BC in their lifetime, and nearly 14.5 million women lived with BC in 2014. This figure is expected to rise to almost 19 million by 2024. Therapeutic options for BC include chemotherapy, radiotherapy, surgery, hormone therapy, and immunotherapy that block tumor cell growth, proliferation, and invasiveness. However, these treatments have little effect on clinical practice. Anticancer vaccine therapy is more tumor-specific and less harmful to normal cells. , Anticancer vaccines can eliminate cancer cells by activating the innate and antibody-mediated immune responses. Following the injection of the vaccine, the immune response is activated by antigen phagocytosis and its processing by antigen-presenting cells (APCs). APCs insert antigens into major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I to activate T-cell-mediated cytotoxicity and inert antigen into MHC class II to activate T-helper cell response and humoral immunity. - In our previous studies, we generated the C-terminal domain of GRP78 via in silico tools. We further accredit this antigen based on the experimental data through ELISA and CD analysis. The results showed that the 3D structure of the recombinant protein is very similar to the intact protein structure. This truncated protein could be a good candidate for an anti-cancer vaccine. Unlike most BC vaccines that are against HER2, which covers a small proportion of patients. The cGRP78-based vaccine can be used for all cancers. This study aims to develop a cancer vaccine based on cGRP78 and evaluate its efficacy in a breast cancer model. Mouse immunization with cGRP78 To investigate the performance of cGRP78 recombinant protein as an anti-breast cancer vaccine, 3-4 weeks old male BALB/c mice were randomly divided into two test and control groups. After a week of adaptation of the mice to the environment, vaccine injections were started in the test and control groups. Vaccines were administered via subcutaneous and peritoneal injections in the left flank. For the first time, 50 μg cGRP78/mice in the test group and PBS in the control group with complete Freund's adjuvant were injected. Two other boosters were injected ten days apart, similar to the first injection, except Freund's complete adjuvant was replaced with Freund's incomplete adjuvant. Before each vaccine injection, blood was collected from four anesthetized mice via a capillary tube in the left eye in the test and control groups. One week after finishing the last vaccine booster, four mice from each group were sacrificed to isolate the spleen for cytokine and cell proliferation tests. Detection of antibody response to cGRP78 by ELISA The reaction of the humoral immune system of mice vaccinated with cGRP78 was measured by the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) technique. Briefly, 96-well plates with 5 μg/well of cGRP78 protein were coated in the coating buffer (carbonate bicarbonate buffer), and after washing, 5% skim milk (Merck, Germany) was used to block the wells. Serial dilutions were prepared from the sera of immunized and control mice (1:100, 1:200, 1:500, and 1:1000) and exposed to cGRP78 for one hour with triplicate repetitions. After washing, HRP (horseradish peroxidase) conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (Sigma-Aldrich, USA) with a dilution of 1:50 000 was added in the wells, and TMB (3, 3’, 5, 5’tetramethylbenzidine) (Merck, Germany) was used to track the bound antibodies. At the end of the reaction, after stopping the reaction with H2SO4, absorbance was measured at 450 nm with an Elisa Reader (Bio-Rad, model 680, California, USA). Cytokine assay and splenocyte proliferation Splenocytes from sacrificed mice were isolated from vaccinated and control mice under sterile conditions, and their cells were extracted. Red blood cells were removed with RBC lysis buffer, and the rest of the cells were cultured in Roswell Park Memorial Institute medium (RPMI) (Gibco, USA) medium supplemented with 10% FBS. 2×10 6 cells from splenocytes of the vaccinated and control groups were cultured in a 24-well plate with 20 μg/mL cGRP78 as a stimulating antigen for 72 hours. IL-2 and IFNγ were evaluated to measure the growth stimulation of cGRP78 antigen on T helper cells and specific Th2 cytokines, including IL-4, IL-6, and IL-10, measured by the ELISA method and particular kits. The growth-stimulating potency of the cGRP78 antigen on spleen lymphocytes was evaluated by the MTT test. The isolated splenocytes of the vaccinated and control groups were cultured at a density of 1×10 5 cells/well in a 96-well plate with 20 μg/mL of cGRP78 antigen cultured in a complete medium. After 72 hours, the MTT solution was added to the wells and incubated for 4 hours. Then the medium on the cells was removed, and DMSO was used to dissolve the formazan crystals. The amount of color produced was evaluated at a wavelength of 570 nm with an ELISA reader. All experiments were performed in triplicate. APCs are activated against these antigens and can be used in cancer immunotherapy. One member of the sizeable HSP70 family is the 78-kDa protein GRP78, which binds to the hydrophobic residues of unfolded polypeptides in the ER and prevents their accumulation. However, in cancer tissues, because of the increased expression of GRP78 and its placement on the surface of cancer cells, this antigen is a good candidate for cancer immunotherapy. Many researchers have developed antibodies against different epitopes of GRP78 and reported the results of using these antibodies. In one study, antibodies against the carboxyl domain of GRP78 in melanoma and prostate cells induced p53 and apoptosis in these cells. Using a high-affinity Mab-159 monoclonal antibody (Kd = 1.7 nmol/L) against surface GRP78 in colon cancer and breast carcinoma cells has inhibited proliferation in these cells. In a wide range of tumors, such as lung, hepatocellular carcinoma, prostate cancer, and breast cancer, high expression of GRP78 induces resistance to a wide range of pharmaceutical agents. - Inhibition of GRP78 causes tumors to become sensitive to drug therapy. As a result, it can be suggested that immunotherapy with cGRP78 could limit the rate of tumor growth and increasing the survivability of mice with breast tumors. After vaccinating mice with the cGRP78 protein, the spleens of vaccinated and unvaccinated mice were isolated to examine the stimulatory effect of this antigen on immune cells. In this study, an MTT assay was used to measure the suppressive or proliferation effects of the cGRP78 antigen on splenocytes. This antigen notably enhanced the proliferative response of the vaccinated mice's splenocytes more noticeably than the non-vaccinated mice's splenocytes, which shows the cGRP78 vaccine has a stimulation effect on the growth and proliferation of immune cells. In the next step, a cytokine assay was performed to evaluate the response of immune cells to the cGRP78 antigen. In this test, five cytokines (IL-2, IFN-γ, TGF-β, IL-6, and IL-10) were assessed, with the results shown in . Previous studies show that IFN-γ levels are associated with an anti-tumor response of the immune system. Macrophages and NK cells (Natural killer cells) are essential in producing the anti-malignant cell response to eliminate tumor cells. NK cells secrete IFN-γ to activate the immune system against tumor cells and induce apoptosis in cancer cells. IFN-γ is also directly related to the activation of the anti-angiogenesis response. - The results showed that IFN-γ levels in cGRP78-immunized mice were significantly higher than in unimmunized mice. As a result, it can be concluded that increased secretion of IFN-γ by immune cells in vaccinated mice causes more apoptosis of cancer cells and slows down the metastasis process in these cells. Introduction Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is one of the most prevalent urological conditions, with an estimated annual healthcare cost of approximately $1.1 billion in the United States ( ). BPH is a leading contributor for the development of lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) in men as they age. It is estimated that the prevalence of BPH at autopsy is as high as 50% to 60% for males in their 60s and that rate increases to 80% to 90% for men over the age of 70 years ( ). Holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) has emerged as a durable, effective, and minimally invasive treatment option for men with BPH ( , ). Despite the success of HoLEP in men with BPH, it is not without postoperative side effects. Both sexual and non-sexual related side effects have been documented ( , ). Additionally, growing awareness of these sexual consequences has contributed to the development of minimally invasive surgical therapies (MISTs), such as UroLift, Rezūm, and Aquablation, which emphasize preservation of antegrade ejaculation, albeit with trade-offs in long-term durability ( ). Given the increasing importance of sexual outcomes in patient-centered decision-making, a focused review of the sexual side effects of HoLEP is needed. This review synthesizes current evidence on HoLEP-related ejaculatory, erectile, and orgasmic changes and evaluates their clinical relevance within the broader landscape of BPH surgical options. We present this article in accordance with the Narrative Review reporting checklist (available at https://tau.amegroups.com/article/view/10.21037/tau-2025-735/rc ). Methods A search of the medical literature was carried out in PubMed and Medline to identify peer-reviewed, original research and systematic reviews on the side effect profile of HoLEP, particularly the sexual side effect profile. The search included all publications from database inception through October 2025. The strategy combined both Medical subject headings (MeSH) and free-text keywords to capture three conceptual domains: (I) BPH (including terms such as “prostatic hyperplasia”, “benign prostatic hyperplasia”, “BPH”, “prostate enlargement”, and “lower urinary tract symptoms”); (II) the HoLEP procedure (including “holmium laser enucleation of the prostate”, “holmium laser enucleation”, “HoLEP”, and variations of the procedural terminology); and (III) postoperative sexual function (including MeSH terms and keywords related to “sexual dysfunction”, “erectile dysfunction”, “ejaculation”, “orgasm”, “penile erection”, “libido”, “sexual satisfaction”, and “sexual side effects”). These three domains were combined using Boolean operators to ensure that all retrieved studies specifically addressed sexual outcomes following HoLEP. No limits were applied for study design, comparator group, or publication type. Language limits were not applied during the initial search; instead, English-language availability was determined during screening. The search identified 243 records, all of which were screened after deduplication. Studies were included if they (I) evaluated HoLEP; (II) reported sexual function outcomes using patient-reported measures or validated instruments; and (III) provided original data. Screening was performed by one author. After screening, 216 records were excluded. Twenty-seven full texts were assessed, and 1 were excluded as an editorial commentary. Twenty-six studies were included in the qualitative synthesis ( , ). Discussion Ejaculatory dysfunction Retrograde ejaculation (RE) is a known side effect of transurethral procedures for outlet obstruction, with rates of RE up to 70–80% following transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) ( ). HoLEP is no exception and has reported rates of RE up to 96%, which is significantly higher than TURP ( ). There are two predominant theories for the mechanism of ejaculatory dysfunction in endoscopic surgery for BPH. The first is that under normal anatomy, retrograde passage of semen is prevented by reflex closure of the bladder neck. Endoscopic surgeries for BPH disrupt this mechanism and thus lead to RE ( ). The second theory is that paracollicular and supracollicular tissues, often described as muscularis ejecularis, which are located 1 cm proximal to the verumontanum, are responsible for anterograde ejaculation ( ). RE is variably defined in the literature. Some define RE as reduced volume of anterograde ejaculate during sexual climax, others would define RE as complete absence of semen fluid or detection of semen on a post-ejaculatory urine sample ( - ). As such, there can be a heterogeneity in the reported literature as it pertains to the rates of RE after HoLEP. Because studies use inconsistent definitions, assessment tools (validated vs . non-validated questionnaires), and follow-up intervals, the reported rates of RE after HoLEP vary widely and are not directly comparable across studies. This methodological heterogeneity limits the ability to draw definitive conclusions about the true incidence of RE and complicates interpretation of the literature. Other authors who have assessed sexual outcomes after HoLEP, although not directly measuring postoperative rates of RE, have anecdotally reported a high prevalence and even counsel their patients that the incidence of RE approaches 100% following the procedure ( ). Male sexual health is multifaceted and includes erectile function, libido, capability of orgasm, and ejaculatory function amongst other components. Importantly, the current body of literature contains relatively few prospective studies designed specifically to evaluate sexual function outcomes following HoLEP. Most data are derived from retrospective cohorts or studies where sexual outcomes were secondary endpoints. Moreover, some studies may rely on databases and registry data which use diagnosis codes only, that can underreport, inaccurately code, or not capture nuanced sexual outcomes postoperatively. As such, definitive conclusions should be drawn with caution. Nevertheless, despite the high rates of RE after HoLEP, its mere presence does not seem to have adverse impacts on overall sexual function ( , ). Several studies have demonstrated declines in orgasmic function associated with postoperative RE. Kim et al. reported a high rate of RE following HoLEP and found that more than half of affected men experienced decreased orgasmic intensity ( ). Similarly, Briganti et al. observed a significant decline in orgasmic function attributable to postoperative RE ( ). However, larger cohort studies indicate that RE itself is not independently predictive of diminished sexual satisfaction; rather, satisfaction decreases primarily among men who report being bothered by the loss of antegrade ejaculation ( ). Moreover, prospective evaluations of sexual outcomes after HoLEP have shown that although RE is common, overall sexual function and satisfaction generally remain stable postoperatively ( , ). It is important to counsel patients regarding the high prevalence of RE following HoLEP. A subset of patients—particularly those who are bothered by ejaculatory changes—may experience reductions in orgasmic quality or sexual satisfaction. However, urologists should also recognize that RE, in isolation, does not significantly affect overall sexual function in men. Erectile dysfunction (ED) ED is a recognized potential complication following TURP. Penile erection is mediated by parasympathetic activation of the cavernosal nerves, which release nitric oxide and trigger a cGMP-dependent cascade leading to smooth muscle relaxation, arterial dilation, and cavernosal engorgement ( ). The development of ED after TURP is thought to result primarily from direct or thermal injury to these nerves responsible for erectile function during the resection of prostate tissue. Reported rates of new-onset ED after TURP vary across studies but generally range from 4% to 14% of patients ( - ). There are conflicting reports in regards to the development of ED after HoLEP. However, the majority of the literature seems to indicate that there is little to no impact on erectile function after HoLEP. Some studies, such as those by Elshal et al. and Deslandes et al. , which were a prospective control trial and a multicenter retrospective study, respectively, have identified a small subset of men—particularly those with normal preoperative erectile function—who may experience a mild but statistically significant decrease in erectile function scores after surgery ( , ). Effects on orgasm We have thus far discussed HoLEP and its association with postoperative RE and ED. Both of these outcomes directly influence the male orgasm, which is a complex experience involving erectile function, ejaculatory function, and libido. Multiple studies have evaluated orgasmic perception and sexual satisfaction in men following HoLEP ( , , ). These studies consistently report that HoLEP results in high rates of RE, which can lead to a measurable decline in orgasmic sensation or ejaculatory function. However, overall sexual satisfaction and erectile function are generally not adversely affected ( , , ). Importantly, most men do not find the loss of antegrade ejaculation particularly bothersome, and their overall satisfaction with sexual life remains stable. In our practice, it is also important to note that a number of these men will have preoperative RE or anejaculation due to the size of their prostates, age-related decline, or the side effects of BPH medications ( , ). Elshal et al. performed a prospective study examining sexual function in men undergoing HoLEP ( ). They examined 80 patients after HoLEP at 1 year and found that there was a significant reduction in orgasm perception, although there was no difference compared to control in overall intercourse satisfaction ( ). Similarly, Meng et al. studied 108 men at 6 months post-HoLEP using standardized sexual function questionnaires ( ). They observed a significant increase in the incidence of RE but no significant change in overall sexual function scores ( ). Briganti et al. also examined sexual function in 60 perioperative HoLEP patients at baseline, 12, and 24 months. Similarly, the authors found high rates of RE, which they reported had no negative effect on sexual function ( ). Overall, HoLEP frequently affects ejaculation and may alter orgasmic quality, and while most patients report acceptable sexual outcomes, clinically meaningful changes occur in a subset of men. Men undergoing HoLEP should be counseled that RE is common and may influence orgasmic perception. Although many men maintain stable overall sexual satisfaction, a proportion will experience declines in orgasmic quality or erectile function, particularly if they find the loss of ejaculation bothersome. Thorough preoperative counseling and attention to patient expectations are essential to reducing postoperative regret. Incontinence and non-sexual side effects Complications after HoLEP are not limited to sexual side effects. In general, non-sexual complications following HoLEP are reported to occur between 0.3% to 6% ( ). The most common complications after HoLEP are urinary stress incontinence and urge incontinence. Urinary continence is maintained by the coordinated function of the internal urethral sphincter and the external urethral sphincter, both of which provide urethral coaptation and prevent leakage during increases in abdominal pressure. These sphincteric structures are supported by the puboprostatic ligaments, endopelvic fascia, and levator ani complex, which stabilize the bladder neck and urethra and maintain continence through a dynamic “sling” mechanism. Disruption or irritation of these anatomic supports—from surgical manipulation—can transiently impair sphincter function and contribute to postoperative stress incontinence ( ). These symptoms are most prevalent during the first few months following surgery. However, their frequency decreases significantly over time ( ). One study found the incidence of urinary incontinence post HoLEP was 43%, 15%, and 5.8% at 6 weeks, 3 months, and 1 year follow-up, respectively ( ). According to Krambeck et al. , the prevalence of both stress and urge incontinence drops dramatically by 12 months post-surgery, affecting as few as 2% of patients ( ). Other notable complications following HoLEP include urethral stricture and bladder neck contracture (BNC), though both are relatively uncommon. The incidence of urethral stricture after HoLEP is low, with most studies reporting rates between 1.2% and 5% ( , ). Similarly, BNC occurs infrequently, with reported rates typically ranging from 0.8% to 6.7% ( ). The reported rate of bleeding requiring transfusion after HoLEP ranges from approximately 0.8% to 5%, depending on the patient population and anticoagulation status ( , ). The reported rate of reoperation following HoLEP is low, indicating a durable response. He et al. reported a reoperation rate at 5 years to be around 6.6% ( ). Another large retrospective study of around 1,000 patients reported a reoperation rate of around 3.7% at 5 years ( ). Although the above complications are traditionally classified as non-sexual, several can have important secondary effects on sexual health and overall well-being. Transient or persistent urinary incontinence may lead to embarrassment, avoidance of sexual activity, and reduced sexual confidence ( ). Urethral stricture, while uncommon, can cause voiding dysfunction, discomfort, and patients typically report poor force of ejaculation, reduced ejaculatory volume, and reduced pleasure ( ). Thus, while non-sexual in nature, these complications may still exert meaningful indirect effects on postoperative sexual outcomes and should be considered during preoperative counseling. Surgical approaches to reduce sexual side effects As discussed, RE is a known side effect of TURP and HoLEP. To address this, surgical modifications have been developed to minimize the risk of postoperative RE. These surgical approaches have paralleled the transition in HoLEP techniques, which have evolved from three- and two-lobe to en bloc enucleation techniques ( ). One such approach involves a limited resection, targeting only the median lobe of the prostate ( ). This technique has recently been adapted for use with HoLEP. In a retrospective study, Press et al. reviewed 55 men with a median prostatic lobe who underwent HoLEP with selective enucleation of the median lobe. Postoperative assessment included patient-reported rates of RE. Remarkably, 90% of those who received the limited resection technique preserved anterograde ejaculation ( ). Another surgical technique proposed has been an ejaculatory hood-sparing technique to HoLEP. One small study examined 26 patients who underwent a limited HoLEP resection where tissue >1 cm proximal to the verumontanum was preserved. However, there was no difference in preservation of ejaculatory function between these men and men undergoing standard HoLEP ( ). An additionally modified 2-lobe technique has been discussed in the literature where the mucous membrane of the bladder neck, circular fibers of the internal urinary sphincter, and urethral membrane from the 11 to 1 o’clock position are preserved ( ). The authors of this paper found that the prevalence of RE after HoLEP dropped from around 64% to 33% ( ). Other modified surgical techniques that attempt to minimize RE include an omega-shaped pre-transection of the prostate apex and preservation of the bladder neck as described by Zhang et al. In their study, 165 men underwent HoLEP with this modified technique with a reported rate of RE of 11.52% ( ). These modified surgical techniques to preserve antegrade ejaculation extend beyond HoLEP into urethral-sparing modifications to robot-assisted simple prostatectomy (RASP). By intentionally limiting the extent of resection or altering the classical HoLEP plane, there is a theoretical risk of higher residual obstruction or need for reintervention, which may offset the benefits of ejaculation preservation for some patients. Emerging techniques in HoLEP—including limited median lobe resection, ejaculatory hood sparing, and the modified 2-lobe technique—demonstrate potential for preserving ejaculatory function. Although results vary, previous studies are limited by small populations, and results are bound to vary between surgeons. These emerging techniques illustrate an effort to balance optimal urinary outcomes with preserved sexual function. Surgeons must carefully weigh the potential for improved ejaculatory outcomes against the uncertain long-term durability of symptom relief. Until robust prospective data with longer follow-up are available, these approaches should be considered early-stage, operator-dependent adaptations, and patients should be counseled explicitly about the trade-off between ejaculatory preservation and de-obstructive durability. Alternatives to HoLEP BPH is among the most common urologic conditions, consuming substantial healthcare resources annually ( ). Given the significant financial impact associated with BPH management and treatment, it is unsurprising that the range of therapeutic options continues to expand beyond TURP or HoLEP to address this growing clinical need. There are multiple factors that are taken into consideration when assessing which outlet procedure would be most suitable for a given patient. This includes patient comorbidities, prostate volume, how invasive the procedure is, and patient desired side effect profile. The American Urological Association (AUA) endorses several different minimally invasive treatment options for men who have gland size between 30 and 80 g. These options include Urolift, Rezum, and Aquablation ( ). It is important to note that all three of these options are touted to preserve or at least have a lower risk of impacting sexual function. This includes erectile function and antegrade ejaculation ( , ). A systematic review examining outcomes of more minimally invasive options for BPH found an anejaculation rate of 3% with Rezum and 0% with Urolift. Additionally, the retreatment rate was low for these treatment options, although follow-up was only out to 24 months ( ). While these options for BPH may not be as definitive as HoLEP, they do offer men an option if they are concerned about preserving ejaculatory function. There are other alternatives for men with BPH who may be unfit for surgery. One option includes prostate artery embolization (PAE). There have been a large number of studies that have investigated PAE that have shown both technical and clinical success, which has been defined as improvement in the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) ( - ). Various studies have reported the clinical success rate of around 85% at 12 months and 82% at 1–3 years. However, the literature also seems to indicate a high degree of reintervention rates around 30% to 60% in patients more than 5 years post PAE ( ). Despite this, PAE remains a strong option for men with severe comorbidities who are not candidates for invasive procedures such as HoLEP. Nevertheless, HoLEP consistently demonstrates high satisfaction scores ( ). When compared with TURP, HoLEP has yielded superior IPSS and quality of life scores and greater long-term durability, as evidenced by a lower retreatment rate ( - ). Additionally, when compared directly to minimally invasive options such as Aquablation, HoLEP has been shown to have superior deobstructive efficacy as evidenced by a greater Qmax and PSA outcomes ( ). The armamentarium to treat BPH is large. With the numerous interventions that have come to market and the varying side effect profiles with each one, it is important for the urologist to consider the patient preference, patient comorbidities, durability of the treatment option, and specific side effect profiles to each intervention. Most available studies are single-center retrospective cohorts with relatively small sample sizes, heterogeneous definitions of sexual outcomes, and variable follow-up durations. However, the current evidence evaluating sexual side effects—particularly RE, orgasmic changes, and the small but meaningful risk of postoperative erectile decline—is limited by several factors. Most available studies are single-center retrospective cohorts with relatively small sample sizes, heterogeneous definitions of sexual outcomes, and variable follow-up durations. Finally, the ability to decipher medical terminology by a patient should not be assumed. Discussion Our study analyzed the impact of COVID-19 on Italian urological surgical activity, documenting a 15.35% reduction in all procedures ( p < 0.001) after the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. Considering elective procedures only, the percentage loss was even larger, increasing to 21.09% of the procedures in the pre-COVID period ( p = 0.001). The COVID-19 pandemic is a major challenge for health care systems worldwide. [ ] Since the first reported case in Italy, the exponential growth of COVID-19 cases has rapidly overwhelmed Italian health care systems, resulting in the partial or total suspension of elective activities to reduce the number of patients requiring hospitalization and free up personnel and equipment for SARS-CoV-2 patient care. [ , ] During the initial phase of the outbreak, urological procedures dropped by 78% [ ] ; consequently, urological surgical waiting lists lengthened, with possible repercussions on the health of the patients. [ ] Urolithiasis can lead to severe complications and increase the burden on emergency services if not treated promptly, with 15% of these patients requiring intensive care unit admission despite decompression of the urinary system and antibiotic therapy, and a mortality rate as high as 8% to 10%. Nevertheless, delayed intervention may decrease patient quality of life and increase their distress due to prolonged stent-related irritative symptoms and pain, difficult management of percutaneous nephrostomy, anxiety, and stone growth requiring a more complex or invasive procedure at a later stage. This study investigated the effect of COVID-19 on all procedures for urinary stones performed during emergencies and elections in 9 high-volume centers located in different areas of Italy. It demonstrated the contraction of surgical volumes, specifically for elective procedures, and a prolongation of the WTs. A certain number of differences in surgical indications also emerged, but the overall treatments maintained similar quality, as shown by the analysis of SFR and complication rates. In addition, we did not observe any major differences in the characteristics of the treated patients. Limitations However, this study had some limitations that need to be acknowledged. First, the data were collected retrospectively, which might have led to missing data. This could potentially introduce bias into the data analysis. The absence of a comparison with the post-acute pandemic period is notable, indicating a need for further studies to understand the changes in the urological field as we continue to grapple with the lasting impact of COVID-19. In addition, due to the nature of the study, the use of imaging modalities resulted in heterogeneity, potentially impacting the accuracy of estimated SFRs. Furthermore, owing to the characteristics of the study, we could not evaluate the increase in workload in emergency departments and urological outpatient clinics caused by delayed treatment, stent-related symptoms, and infectious complications. A larger cohort of patients should be enrolled from a wider selection of urological centers to confirm this trend. During Period B, among the urgent cases performed despite patients being positive for COVID-19, we were unable to discern the number of patients with symptomatic infection. Lastly, we could not evaluate whether patients contracted COVID-19 following hospitalization for stone treatment. Our study highlighted how COVID-19 significantly disrupted endourological services for urinary stones nationwide. A reduced number of patients received treatment over an extended period (approximately 1 in 5 patients could not receive treatment). Assessing the actual impact of these delays during the pandemic is challenging, especially concerning the increased risk of renal function loss and infectious complications, such as severe sepsis. The effect on patient’s quality of life remains unclear, necessitating further studies.

1 Introduction The term Post-Acute Sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC), also known as “Long COVID”, refers to numerous conditions associated with widespread morbidity and rising healthcare costs. PASC has highly variable clinical presentations, and likely includes multiple molecular subtypes ( ; ). The NIH-sponsored “Researching COVID to Enhance Recovery” (RECOVER) initiative includes retrospective/prospective cohort studies including an adult cohort ( ), a cohort of pregnant adults ( ; ) and a pediatric cohort ( ; ). These studies aim to enroll a total of 12,580 adult non-pregnant patients, 2,300 adult pregnant patients and 19,300 pediatric patients to rapidly improve our understanding of and ability to predict, treat, and prevent Post-Acute Sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC, or “Long COVID”) through deep clinical phenotyping and laboratory studies. THE RECOVER “OMICS” Task Force was charged with developing recommendations based on published evidence and the experiences of its members, to incorporate multi-omics into the analysis of RECOVER results. 2 Methods 2.1 Objectives The “OMICS” task force of the RECOVER study, a multi-disciplinary committee including clinicians, pathologists, laboratory scientists and data scientists, was charged with developing recommendations to apply cutting-edge system biology technologies to achieve the goals of RECOVER. The task force met biweekly over 14 months, to evaluate published evidence, examine the possible contribution of each “omics” technique to the study of PASC, as well as the potential limitations of each technique, and develop a consensus recommendation. The work was divided into two stages. During the first stage, sub-committees with specific expertise on an “omics” technique examined evidence supporting the use of that technique to study PASC, the type of data it could generate and the mechanistic questions it could answer, based on published evidence and the experiences of its members, to incorporate multi-omics into the analysis of RECOVER results. Each sub-committee presented to the entire task force. During the second stage, the task force combined the findings of each sub-committee into a comprehensive study design recommendation. 3 Results and discussion The OMICS task force recommended that integrated, longitudinal, simultaneous multi-omics studies of participant biospecimens be performed on the entire RECOVER cohort through centralized laboratories, as opposed to multiple smaller studies using one or few analytical techniques. The RECOVER adult protocol ( ) includes multiple biospecimen collections: nasopharyngeal or nasal swab, 2 8.5 mL aliquots of blood in serum separation tubes, 4 × 8 ml aliquots of blood in cell preparation tubes, 2 × 2.7 mL aliquots of blood in sodium citrate tubes for plasma proteomics, 1 × 10 ml aliquot of blood in EDTA tube, 1 2.5 mL aliquot of blood in PAXgene RNA tube, 1 × 10 ml urine (no additives), 1 × 2mL aliquot of saliva in Oragene OGR 600 and 1 25 mL aliquot of stool. Of these, stool is sent by participants while the other samples are processed locally as per protocol specifications and shipped in batches to the central tissue bank. Participants who consent to biospecimen donation for future research are asked to provide blood and nasopharyngeal/nasal swab biospecimens at enrollment, 90 and 180 days after the index date (date of first infection or negative COVID test), and then annually ( ). Saliva is collected upon enrollment for genetic analysis. Urine and stool are collected biannually. Additionally, a battery of clinical laboratory tests is performed in CLIA-certified laboratories at enrollment, 90 and 189 days after the index date, and thereafter, abnormal tests are repeated annually. Specific symptoms or abnormal study results trigger “Tier 2” or “Tier 3” assessments (see ( ) for details). A SARS-CoV-2 PCR test is performed at enrollment for all “uninfected” participants, who are also tested for SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid antibodies spike protein antibodies for unvaccinated participants. In addition to study visits, imaging and laboratory tests, participants complete multiple surveys, using validated survey instruments whenever possible, at 90-day intervals throughout the study. At enrollment, data are collected on demographics, social determinants of health (SDOH), disability, characteristics of the initial SARS-CoV-2 infection (if applicable), pregnancy (if applicable), vaccination status, comorbidities, medications, and PASC symptoms. Subsequently, at 90-day intervals, data are collected on interim infections, time-varying social determinants, vaccinations, comorbidities, medications and symptoms ( ). The PASC symptom survey was developed for RECOVER and includes an overall quality of life instrument (PROMIS-10) and screening for core symptoms (43 for biological males and 46 for biological females) drawn from existing literature plus input from patient representatives and investigators. Questions about depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and grief are also included. Report of a symptom may trigger additional questions about that symptom. Details of survey instruments are in the original reference ( ). The pregnancy study ( ) follows a similar design to the non-pregnant adult study, enrolling participants with suspected, probable or confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection during pregnancy, or documented lack of exposure to SARS-CoV-2 during pregnancy. Data generation and analytical strategies should leverage integrative bioinformatics and machine learning. A major advantage, and a potential challenge, of multi-omics approaches is that datasets derived from different analytical techniques and measured using different scales must be integrated. Approaches including multi-omics integration paired with ML have been gaining popularity in clinical and biomedical research (see ( ; )), though this field is rapidly evolving. An important advantage inherent in multi-dimensional measurements is that the extent to which different measurements agree with each other or not is potentially informative. For instance, transcriptomic data may or may not be reflected in the relative abundance of protein products, or quantitative differences in non-coding RNA expression may or may not translate into relative abundance of potential target mRNAs, the proteins they encode or the metabolites that these proteins may process. System biology approaches based on multi-omics have been used successfully in the study of cardiovascular disease ( ). With respect to PASC, strategies similar to what we propose have been used on a smaller scale. ML has been used in the context of a multi-step analytical strategy to combine proteomic and metabolomic data to generate a multi-omics biomarker predictive of the risk of PASC ( ) and give insights on the metabolic pathways altered during PASC. Dimensionality reduction was achieved through unsupervised cluster analysis followed by autoencoder (AE), using a three-layer neural network. Supervised ML was then used to identify the minimal number of molecules predictive of adverse clinical outcomes.
